query: FeCoNi is an fcc alloy with high saturation magnetization and a low coercive field. Earlier studies examined the high-entropy alloys FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt, but both exhibited soft ferromagnetism. A qualifying high-entropy alloy must have an almost equiatomic multicomponent composition and configurational entropy of at least 1.0R. Subject to these constraints, what single intervention could produce a FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy with greater coercivity than the prior derivatives? Present one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an appropriate FeCoNi-based baseline, defines the conditions over which it should apply, cites supporting observations from earlier work, and proposes a discriminating experiment with an explicit falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: A near-equiatomic FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy subjected to moderate-temperature annealing and rapid quenching will partially order and form nanometric precipitates that enhance domain-wall pinning, producing a measurable increase in coercivity relative to the same alloy in a solution-treated or as-cast state.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast or solution-treated, near-equiatomic FeCoNi-based alloy meeting ≥1.0R configurational entropy criteria.
generation.intervention: Thermal treatment consisting of holding at 500–600 °C followed by rapid quenching.
generation.conditions: Maintain the alloy at 500–600 °C for 1–10 hours in an inert environment or vacuum, then quench (e.g., into water or oil) to freeze in the partially ordered microstructure.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of short-range ordering and finely dispersed precipitates within the fcc matrix.
generation.mechanism: Partial ordering and nano-precipitates create local anisotropy and act as pinning sites, thereby increasing coercivity without significantly reducing saturation magnetization.
generation.predicted_outcome: A roughly three- to four-fold increase in coercivity compared to the as-cast or solution-treated baseline (<10 Oe), while preserving the high-entropy single-phase character and strong magnetization of FeCoNi alloys.
generation.baseline: Solution-treated FeCoNi-based HEA with low coercivity (on the order of a few Oe).
generation.boundary: Over-annealing (e.g., above 600 °C or excessively long times) risks coarsening and loss of in-grain ordering effects, diminishing coercivity gains and potentially reducing configurational entropy.
generation.uncertainty: Exact precipitation morphology and degree of short-range ordering may vary based on alloy purity, exact temperature hold, and quench efficiency, potentially affecting the magnitude of coercivity enhancement.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical near-equiatomic FeCoNi-based alloys. Subject one set to the moderate-temperature annealing and quenching cycle, and retain the other set in the solution-treated state for direct comparison.
measurements: Measure X-ray diffraction or electron diffraction patterns to confirm any partial ordering or new phases.
Compare coercivity and saturation magnetization using vibrating-sample magnetometry for both sets.
Assess microstructure (grain size, precipitate size, short-range order) via transmission electron microscopy.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed and quenched samples do not exhibit higher coercivity than the solution-treated baseline under identical measurement conditions, the hypothesis is refuted.

In summary, we have achieved high magnetic anisotropy in rare‐earth‐free high entropy metallic thin films by sputtering and RTA. Robust magnetic order of both fcc FeCoNiMnCu and L10 (FeCoNiMnCu)Pt films has been demonstrated. The FeCoNiMnCu films exhibit a large coercivity increase after RTA, resulting from microstructural changes and strain‐induced anisotropy enhancement which strengthens domain wall pinning. Addition of Pt reduces the symmetry of the cubic fcc lattice to an intermetallic tetragonal L10 phase of (FeCoNiMnCu)Pt. Although the Pt insertion lowers the configurational entropy compared to the equiatomic case, the entropy is still high enough to stabilize an L10 single phase. This intermetallic phase is confirmed to host high magnetocrystalline anisotropy, likely attributed to the lower symmetry of the L10 structure and the strong spin‐orbit coupling provided by the Pt insertion. These findings demonstrate the promise of high‐entropy intermetallic design as a key avenue to search for new high‐entropy magnets beyond the equiatomic composition.

The saturation magnetization (MS) and coercivity (Hc) for the four different samples analyzed in the present study have been listed in Table 1. The MS of AlCoFeNi is substantially higher compared to that of the AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi alloy for both heat-treated conditions. While the magnetization is primarily determined by composition and the crystal structure, the coercivity can be affected by impurities, deformation, grain size and phase decomposition. The coercivity (Hc) decreased with increasing annealing temperature from 15 Oe for sample aged at 600 °C/15 h, exhibiting nanoscale phase separation, to 4 Oe for samples aged at 1000 °C/15 h, exhibiting a homogeneous undecomposed B2 matrix. A similar observation has been reported in the literature, where the coercivity of the AlCoCrCuFeNi HEA annealed at 1000 °C/2 h decreases by 30 Oe (from 45 Oe to 15 Oe) compared to as-cast alloys. The AlCoFeNi HEA investigated in the present study exhibits higher saturation magnetization and lower coercivity than other soft ferrite magnetic materials, e.g., MnZn ferrite, Cu-Zn-Ti ferrite,, as revealed in Supplementary Table 2.

decision.trend: Over several FeCoNi-based HEA studies, researchers have added various elements or employed specialized processing to alter microstructure and magnetic storage. First, solidification under a strong static magnetic field was used to fine-tune grains in FeCoNi(AlSi)0.2 (PMC7512793), yielding improved soft magnetic behavior but not significantly higher coercivity. Next, partial Cr substitution in AlCoFeNi (PMC6197204) demonstrated that adding an element can boost coercivity—but at the expense of reduced saturation magnetization. More recently, post-deposition rapid thermal annealing (RTA) of FeCoNiMnCu-based thin films with Pt additions (PMC11267332) formed a single-phase L10 alloy with strongly enhanced anisotropy, providing a large coercivity increase. Although these approaches revealed the value of structural ordering for raising coercivity, maintaining the base FeCoNi system in a nearly equiatomic, single-phase high-entropy regime at or above 1.0R entropy remains an open challenge, especially without resorting to new alloying additions.
decision.unsolved: It is still unclear how to induce sufficient magnetic anisotropy and domain-wall pinning in a nearly equiatomic FeCoNi-based HEA to achieve a marked rise in coercivity while maintaining high entropy and strong magnetization, without introducing additional elements.
decision.lever: Impose a moderate-temperature annealing step (e.g., 500–600 °C) to partially order the fcc matrix and induce controlled nanometric precipitates or short-range ordering that enhance domain-wall pinning, followed by rapid cooling to freeze in these features.
decision.why: Prior studies (e.g., PMC11267332) show that inducing atomic-scale ordering can substantially increase magnetic anisotropy, while short-range or partial ordering in an fcc FeCoNi system could raise coercivity without requiring new alloying elements. A moderate annealing temperature and subsequent quench can stabilize nano-domains that impede domain-wall motion, thus boosting coercivity while preserving high saturation magnetization and high configurational entropy. A discriminating experiment would compare the magnetization hysteresis loops of isochemically identical FeCoNi-based samples with and without the precisely controlled annealing/quenching protocol. A true increase in coercivity would confirm the effect; if no significant change is observed, the hypothesis of partial ordering–induced domain-wall pinning would be falsified.
